title: “GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR I’LL DIE!” — THE DESPERATE CRY OF A WOMAN WHO HAD EVERYTHING EXCEPT WHAT HER HEART WANTED MOST
paragraphs: “GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR I’LL DIE!” — THE DESPERATE CRY OF A WOMAN WHO HAD EVERYTHING EXCEPT WHAT HER HEART WANTED MOST

Rachel was loved by Jacob, but love could not silence the ache of her empty womb. Behind her desperate words in Genesis 30:1 lies a devastating story of jealousy, unanswered prayers, wounded identity, and a God who remembers people even when heaven seems silent. And somewhere in Rachel’s story, you may recognize the pain you have never dared to tell anyone.
There are cries that come from your mouth.
And there are cries that come from a place so deep inside your soul that even you are frightened by what you hear yourself saying.
Rachel had reached that place.

She was not standing before an enemy. She was standing before the man who loved her. The man who had worked seven years to marry her, only to be deceived into marrying her sister first, and then agreed to another seven years of service for her sake.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Scripture makes that unmistakably clear.
But there was something his love could not give her.
Something she watched other women experience while she waited.
Something that turned ordinary family moments into painful reminders of what she did not have.
And one day, the anguish she had been carrying finally erupted.
“Give me children, or else I die.” — Genesis 30:1, KJV
Read those words again.
Not as a religious quotation.
Not as a familiar Bible verse.
Hear them as the anguished words of a real woman who had reached the edge of her emotional endurance.
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Imagine the silence that followed.
Imagine Jacob looking at the woman he loved, hearing a demand that no husband could fulfill by his own power.
Imagine Rachel standing there with tears, resentment, and desperation tangled together.
She had a husband who loved her.
She had a place in his household.
She had the affection her sister desperately wanted.
But every time Leah held another child, Rachel was confronted with the one blessing she longed to receive.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the most difficult suffering is not having nothing.
It is having so much to be thankful for while one unanswered longing threatens to swallow your gratitude whole.
You can have a family and still feel lonely.
You can have a career and still feel insignificant.
You can be surrounded by people celebrating their answered prayers while privately wondering whether God has forgotten yours.
You can genuinely love Jesus and still find yourself crying over something you cannot change.
And if you have ever whispered, “Lord, I am thankful for what You have given me, but why does this still hurt so much?” then Rachel’s story deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves your attention.
Because Genesis 30 is not merely about a woman who wanted children.
It is about what can happen when a legitimate longing becomes so consuming that we begin to believe we cannot live without its fulfillment.
And it is about the God who sees human suffering without surrendering His sovereignty to human desperation.
To understand Rachel’s cry, we must return to the wounds that existed before she ever spoke those words.
Jacob entered the household of Laban and fell in love with Rachel.
Genesis 29:20 tells us that he served seven years for her, and those years seemed like only a few days because of his love.
Seven years.
Think about that.
Seven years of labor, anticipation, and hope.
But on the wedding night, Laban deceived Jacob and gave him Leah instead.
When morning came, Jacob discovered the deception.
Rachel eventually became Jacob’s wife as well, but the household was already marked by betrayal, rivalry, and the consequences of human manipulation.
And the Bible does not romanticize what followed.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Leah knew it.
Rachel knew it.
And God saw it.
Genesis 29:31 says:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” — KJV

The Hebrew word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the verb sane, meaning “to hate.” In this family context, the contrast with Jacob's greater love for Rachel shows Leah was the less-loved wife. The passage does not require us to imagine that Jacob felt nothing but hostility toward her. It does, however, expose the painful reality of her rejection.
Leah was living beside a woman who received the affection she longed for.
Rachel was living beside a woman who received the children she longed for.
One had the greater share of Jacob’s affection.
The other was bearing his sons.
And both women were suffering.
Do you see the tragedy?
Two sisters lived under the same roof, each looking at the other and seeing the thing she believed would finally make her whole.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Rachel wanted to become a mother.
And neither woman's deepest wound could be healed merely by taking what the other possessed.
This is one of the quiet cruelties of comparison.
It can make another person's blessing feel like an accusation against your life.
Someone announces a pregnancy, and you smile while your heart breaks.
Someone gets married, and you congratulate them while wondering why you are still alone.
Someone receives the opportunity you have prayed for, and suddenly their joy awakens your disappointment.
You do not necessarily hate them.
You may sincerely rejoice with them.
But somewhere beneath that joy is an aching question.
“God, when will it be my turn?”
And perhaps the most exhausting part is the guilt that follows.
Because you know you should be grateful.
You know other people are suffering too.
You know God has already been good to you.
Yet the ache remains.
Rachel knew what it was to watch someone else receive what she desperately wanted.
Genesis 30:1 begins with a revealing statement:
“And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister...” — KJV
Notice the sequence.
Rachel saw.
Rachel envied.
Rachel spoke.
What she repeatedly saw became entangled with what she believed about herself.
And what she believed eventually erupted in her marriage.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתְּקַנֵּא רָחֵל בַּאֲחֹתָהּ
Vatteqanne Rachel ba'achotah.
“And Rachel envied her sister.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root קנא (q-n-ʾ), associated with jealousy, envy, or zeal, depending on context.
Here the meaning is unmistakable.
Rachel was not simply grieving her infertility.
She was envying Leah.
That distinction matters.
Because grief and envy are not the same thing.
Grief says, “I am hurting because something precious is missing.”
Envy says, “I am hurting because someone else has what I want.”
Grief needs compassion.
Envy needs to be confronted with truth.
And sometimes both live in the same wounded heart.
That does not make your pain imaginary.
It means your pain must not be allowed to become the ruler of your soul.
Perhaps this is where the Holy Spirit is pressing gently but firmly upon something you have avoided.
You have been calling it disappointment.
But somewhere along the way, disappointment became resentment.
You have been calling it waiting.
But somewhere along the way, waiting became bitterness.
You have been calling it a desire.
But somewhere along the way, that desire began to determine whether you believed God was good.
And now, every testimony that should remind you of His faithfulness feels like another reminder of your unanswered prayer.
Rachel's words reveal what happens when longing begins to speak with the authority of life and death.
The Hebrew of Genesis 30:1 reads:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve'im-ayin, metah anokhi.
A close translation is:
“Give me sons, and if not, I am dying.”

The word בָנִים (vanim) literally means “sons,” although the broader sense in the narrative concerns Rachel's desire for children. The Hebrew expression translated “I am dying” communicates the extremity of her anguish. It does not establish that Rachel was physically dying or that she intended to take her own life.
Her words were desperate.
They were emotionally charged.
And they placed an impossible demand upon Jacob.
Rachel was effectively saying that life without children had become unbearable to her.
But Jacob was not God.
And he knew it.
Genesis 30:2 records his angry response:
“Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” — KJV
Jacob's anger was not an example of ideal tenderness toward a suffering wife.
His words, however, exposed a theological truth.
He did not possess the authority to open Rachel's womb.
He could not manufacture the blessing she demanded.
He could not occupy God's place.
And here is a difficult question worth asking.
Have you ever demanded from a human being what only God can ultimately give?
Have you expected a spouse to heal every insecurity?
A child to give your life meaning?
A relationship to rescue you from loneliness?
Success to finally convince you that you matter?
A ministry to prove that God is pleased with you?
There is nothing inherently sinful about longing for marriage, children, healing, provision, or meaningful work.
These can be beautiful gifts.
But even beautiful gifts become dangerous when we ask them to carry the weight of our ultimate hope.
No husband can be God.
No wife can be God.
No child can be God.
No promotion, ministry, financial breakthrough, or human approval can be God.
And when we make a created blessing the condition of our willingness to live with hope, we are placing upon that blessing a burden it was never designed to bear.
Rachel needed more than a child.
She needed to know that her life was not worthless without one.
And somebody reading this needs to hear the same truth.
Your worth is not measured by the blessing you have not received.
You are not less human because you are unmarried.
You are not less valuable because you have no children.
You are not spiritually inferior because your healing has not come.
You are not forgotten because another person's prayer was answered before yours.
And you do not need to pretend that the absence does not hurt in order to believe those things.
The God of Scripture never requires us to confuse faith with emotional dishonesty.
The Psalms contain cries of anguish.
Hannah wept bitterly before the Lord because she had no children.
Job lamented the day of his birth amid terrible suffering.
Even our Lord Jesus, in Gethsemane, expressed profound sorrow while submitting Himself perfectly to the Father's will.
Biblical faith is not the absence of tears.
It is bringing our tears before the true God rather than allowing our pain to define Him.
But Rachel's story becomes even more complicated.
After confronting Jacob, she offered him her servant Bilhah so that Bilhah could bear children within the household on Rachel's behalf.
This arrangement belonged to the ancient social world of Genesis, where enslaved women could be used to produce heirs for a household.
We must not turn that historical description into a moral endorsement.
Bilhah was a person, not merely an instrument in Rachel's struggle.
And the narrative shows how rivalry and household arrangements involving unequal power could deepen an already fractured family.
Bilhah bore sons.
Rachel named the first Dan, connecting his birth with her sense that God had judged her case and heard her voice.
The second she named Naphtali.
Genesis 30:8 records Rachel saying:
“With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.” — KJV
Wrestlings.
With her sister.
Think about the sorrow of that sentence.
A child had been born into the household, and Rachel described the event in the language of struggle and victory over Leah.
The desire for motherhood had become entangled with a competition.
And the competition was tearing through relationships that should never have been reduced to a contest.
This is what envy does when left unchecked.
It changes the meaning of blessings.
A blessing becomes a score.
A relationship becomes a rivalry.
A person's joy becomes evidence of your defeat.
And even when you finally receive something you wanted, you may discover that winning the comparison has not brought peace.
Because the problem was never simply that someone else had more.
The deeper problem was that comparison had begun to tell you who you were.
If this is touching a hidden place in your heart, do not rush past it.
You do not have to publicly reveal private details. But you can be spiritually honest.
Maybe your prayer today is simply, “Lord, heal the envy I have been hiding beneath my pain.”
And if that is your struggle, you are not the only one.
The Gospel does not invite us to deny our sin or despair over it.
It calls us to bring both our sin and our sorrow to Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus did not come merely to comfort people who had been hurt.
He came to save sinners.
People who had envied.
People who had manipulated.
People who had spoken cruelly.
People who had made idols out of good things.
People who had wounded others while trying to soothe their own wounds.
People like the family in Genesis.
People like us.

And then, after all the conflict, after all the rivalry, after all the complicated attempts to build a family through human arrangements, Scripture gives us one of the most tender turns in Rachel's story.
Genesis 30:22 says:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.” — KJV
Stop there.
God remembered Rachel.
The Hebrew reads:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“And God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew verb זכר (zakhar) means “to remember.”
But when Scripture speaks of God remembering someone, it does not mean He had previously forgotten that person's existence and suddenly recalled it.
God is not subject to human forgetfulness.
In passages such as Genesis 8:1, where God remembers Noah, and Exodus 2:24, where God remembers His covenant, divine remembrance is connected with God's faithful attention and action.
In Rachel's case, the text immediately explains what happened.
God listened to her.
And God opened her womb.
The turning point is attributed to God, not to Rachel's rivalry, not to Jacob's ability, and not to a technique that could force heaven's hand.
Rachel conceived and gave birth to Joseph.
Genesis 30:23 records her words:
“God hath taken away my reproach.” — KJV
For a woman who had carried the social shame of infertility in her ancient setting, the birth of Joseph was profoundly significant.
Her long-awaited child was born.
Her sorrow had met a remarkable answer.
But there is something we must be careful not to do with this beautiful moment.
We must not tell every woman experiencing infertility that God will certainly give her a biological child if she prays long enough.
We must not tell every grieving parent that faith guarantees another baby.
We must not tell every unmarried believer that marriage is waiting just around the corner.
We must not turn Rachel's testimony into a promise God never made to every individual.
Rachel's story reveals God's power and His particular mercy in her life.
It does not give us authority to predict the precise outcome of another person's suffering.
And this matters because false promises can wound people who are already bleeding.
Some believers have prayed for years and have not conceived.
Some have endured miscarriages.
Some have buried children.
Some have longed for marriage and remained single.
Some have prayed for physical healing while continuing to live with illness.
Their unanswered longings are not proof that God loves them less.
And their suffering is not permission for others to accuse them of insufficient faith.
God remembered Rachel.
But God's faithful love toward His people is not measured only by whether He grants the particular earthly outcome they desire.
The clearest revelation of that love is Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we finally became emotionally healthy.
Not after we stopped struggling with envy.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after our prayers were answered.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And it changes everything.
Because Rachel's story is not the final word of Scripture.
Her son Joseph would become a central figure in God's preservation of Jacob's family through famine.
And through the larger history of Israel, God would continue His covenant purposes until the coming of Jesus Christ.
Jesus came through the line of Judah, Leah's son, not through Rachel's son Joseph.
Let that truth settle into your heart.
The sister who felt less loved became the mother of Judah, from whose line the Messiah would come.
And Rachel, who endured the anguish of infertility, became the mother of Joseph, whom God would later use to preserve many lives.
Neither woman could see the full reach of God's purposes from the place where she was hurting.
Neither woman's suffering made her disposable.
Neither woman's value depended upon defeating the other.
And God's purposes were greater than the competition that had consumed their household.
This is not an invitation to pretend their wounds were necessary or that every human wrong was good.
The deception, favoritism, jealousy, and exploitation in this family were real.
But God was not defeated by their failures.
He continued His redemptive work amid deeply flawed people.
And that is the kind of God we encounter throughout Scripture.
A God who does not excuse sin.
A God who does not abandon His covenant purposes because human beings are broken.
A God who brings redemption where human beings have created wreckage.
A God whose grace is greater than the scandals of the people He calls.
And nowhere is that grace revealed more fully than at the cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our fallen world.
He was rejected.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He suffered.
He was crucified.
And He rose again.
Not merely to improve our circumstances.
Not merely to give us the earthly blessings we have been waiting for.
But to reconcile sinners to God, defeat death, and give eternal life to those who trust in Him.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to “Your breakthrough is coming.”
Sometimes the breakthrough we demand is not the deepest rescue we need.
Sometimes God answers with a gift.
Sometimes He sustains us through an absence.
Sometimes He changes our circumstances.
Sometimes He transforms us while the circumstances remain painfully unchanged.
But the crucified and risen Christ offers something no earthly blessing can guarantee.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A living hope.
And a future in which death, mourning, crying, and pain will not have the final word.
That hope does not make today's grief insignificant.
It makes today's grief something we can bring before a Savior who understands suffering.
And there is another heartbreaking detail in Rachel's story that many readers overlook.
Joseph was not the end of her life.
Years later, Rachel conceived again.
But during the birth of Benjamin, she experienced severe labor and died.
Genesis 35:18 tells us that as her life was departing, she named the child Ben-oni, a name commonly understood as “son of my sorrow,” while Jacob named him Benjamin.
The woman who once cried, “Give me children, or else I die,” eventually died in childbirth.
That is a sobering part of the biblical account.
And we must handle it with care.
Scripture does not say Rachel's death was divine punishment for her earlier desperate words.
We have no right to claim that.
Nor should we turn her death into a simplistic warning against wanting children.
Her desire for motherhood was not itself evil.
The tragedy reminds us instead of how fragile human life is and how inadequate earthly fulfillment is as the foundation of ultimate hope.
Rachel received the children she longed for.
Yet even motherhood could not make her immune to suffering and death.
No earthly gift can.
Not even the gift you have spent years praying to receive.
This is why Jesus must be more than the One we approach to obtain our desires.
He must become our Savior, Lord, and greatest treasure.
Because one day, every earthly blessing will reveal its limits.
Health can fail.
Relationships can change.
Money can disappear.
Beauty fades.
Careers end.
Even the people we love most cannot remain with us forever in this present life.
But Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
And His resurrection means death does not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
Perhaps you began reading this article because Rachel's desperate cry caught your attention.
But perhaps you have stayed because there is a desperate cry of your own.
“Lord, give me a child.”
“Lord, save my marriage.”
“Lord, heal my body.”
“Lord, bring my son home.”
“Lord, restore my daughter.”
“Lord, help me find work.”
“Lord, take away this loneliness.”
“Lord, forgive what I have done.”
“Lord, I am so tired of waiting.”
And perhaps the hardest prayer of all:
“Lord, what if the answer I want never comes?”
That is not a question to answer carelessly.
No short religious phrase can erase the ache of years of longing.
But there is a truth sturdy enough to hold you while you wrestle.
God's goodness is not on trial every time your circumstances remain unresolved.
The cross has already revealed the depth of His love.
The empty tomb has already declared that death is not sovereign.
And His Word gives you permission to lament without making despair your master.
You can cry and still trust.
You can wait and still worship.
You can confess envy and receive forgiveness.
You can admit disappointment without abandoning faith.
You can seek medical help, wise counsel, prayer, and the support of your church without treating those things as evidence of spiritual failure.
You can rejoice with others while asking God to heal the part of your heart that aches.
And you can surrender an unanswered desire to Christ without pretending that surrender is easy.
Surrender is not always a dramatic moment at an altar.
Sometimes surrender looks like opening your eyes in the morning and saying:
“Jesus, I still want what I wanted yesterday. It still hurts. I still do not understand. But I will not make this unanswered prayer greater than You.”
Sometimes repentance looks like apologizing to someone whose joy you resented.
Sometimes healing begins with admitting that you have been comparing your life with people whose private battles you cannot see.
Sometimes faith looks like refusing to measure God's affection by another person's blessings.
And sometimes spiritual maturity looks like learning to say:
“Lord, if You give me this gift, help me receive it with gratitude. If You do not, help me remain faithful to You.”
That prayer is not resignation to a cruel fate.
It is trust in the character of a good and sovereign Father.
And it echoes the submission of Jesus in Gethsemane:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Jesus did not speak those words from a place of comfort.
He spoke them as He faced the suffering of the cross.
His obedience was not painless.
But it was perfect.
And through His obedience, sinners like us can receive grace.
So perhaps the most important question Rachel's story leaves with us is not simply, “Will God give me what I am asking for?”
Perhaps it is this:
“If God does not give me what I am asking for, will I still believe that Jesus Christ is enough to save me, sustain me, and lead me home?”
Do not answer too quickly.
Let the question search you.
Because some of us have spent so much time asking God to change our circumstances that we have neglected to ask Him to change our hearts.
We want relief.
He calls us to Himself.
We want control.
He calls us to trust.
We want our story to unfold according to our preferred ending.
He calls us to follow the Savior who has already conquered the grave.
And when we come to Him, we do not come pretending to be stronger than we are.
We come as needy people.
Sinners in need of mercy.
Wounded people in need of compassion.
Believers in need of daily grace.
Jesus does not promise that discipleship will remove every painful longing.
But He does call the weary to come to Him.
And the Gospel assures us that those who belong to Him are not condemned in Christ Jesus.
Your pain is not your identity.
Your infertility is not your identity.
Your singleness is not your identity.
Your past failure is not your identity.
Your unanswered prayer is not your identity.
For those united to Christ by faith, their deepest identity is found in Him.
Loved by grace.
Redeemed through His blood.
Called to holiness.
Held by a Savior whose faithfulness does not expire when circumstances become difficult.
That is the transformation the Gospel brings.
Not the denial of pain.
Not the glorification of suffering.
But a new life centered upon Jesus Christ.
And before you leave this story, I want to ask you something personal.
What is the one unanswered prayer that has been shaping the way you see yourself?
What is the one blessing you have watched others receive while you have struggled to celebrate with them?
What is the one longing you are afraid to surrender because you worry surrender means losing hope?
You do not have to expose the most private details of your life to strangers.
But you can take one honest step toward prayer and community today.
Someone reading may need to know that faith can survive a long season of unanswered prayer.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is possible after bitterness.
Someone may need to discover that their life still has meaning in Christ even when it looks nothing like the life they imagined.
Your honesty could help another person find the courage to seek God.
And if someone came to your mind while you were reading, do not ignore them.
Perhaps it is a friend who has struggled with infertility.
Perhaps it is a married couple silently grieving.
Perhaps it is someone who has become bitter after watching others prosper.
Perhaps it is a believer who still attends church but privately wonders whether God hears their prayers.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, recognize their need for repentance, receive encouragement to trust Jesus, and grow in discipleship.
Not merely another place to collect inspiring words.
A place to be reminded that Jesus Christ is worthy of our trust even when life hurts.
And there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
It is not a purchase of spiritual favor.
It is not proof that you love Jesus more than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it is not a replacement for your responsibility to support your local church.
Biblical giving must never be manipulated by fear, guilt, or promises that God will answer prayers in exchange for money.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
You can glorify God through generous stewardship, just as you can glorify Him through prayer, service, hospitality, faithful witness, and caring for those in need.
These products are not what makes discipleship meaningful.
Christ does.
They are simply another way to encourage biblical reflection, express faith, and help sustain the work.
The goal is to see people growing in the truth of God's Word, confessing sin, trusting Christ, loving their neighbors, and persevering in faith.
Because what would it profit us to build an audience if we failed to point that audience to the Savior?
We do not want people to become dependent on Gospel Warrior.
We want them to become deeply rooted in Jesus Christ.
And now, before this story ends, return with me one last time to Rachel.
Picture her standing before Jacob.
A woman overwhelmed by longing.
A woman wounded by comparison.
A woman who had confused the absence of one precious gift with the collapse of her entire life.
“Give me children, or else I die.”
We know that God eventually gave Rachel Joseph.
We know that her life also contained sorrow beyond that answered prayer.
And we know that her story became part of a much greater biblical history that ultimately leads us to the hope revealed in Jesus Christ.
But we must not leave Rachel trapped in that one desperate sentence.
She was more than her envy.
More than her infertility.
More than her anguish.
More than the most painful words she ever spoke.
And you are more than the worst thing you have ever felt, feared, wanted, or said.
There is grace for the repentant sinner.
There is mercy for the weary.
There is forgiveness through the blood of Christ.
There is hope beyond the blessings this world can give.
And there is a Savior who does not require you to repair yourself before coming to Him.
So come to Jesus.
Bring the longing.
Bring the jealousy you are ashamed to admit.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the prayers you have repeated until your voice feels empty.
Bring the anger you need to confess.
Bring the grief you have carried alone.
Ask Him to forgive your sins.
Ask Him to teach you to trust His Word.
Ask Him to help you desire His glory more than your own preferred outcome.
And remember that your life is not suspended until one particular prayer is answered.
You can love today.
You can serve today.
You can worship today.
You can repent today.
You can receive and extend grace today.
You can live faithfully today.
Not because your circumstances are perfect.
But because Jesus Christ is alive.
And if you have reached the end of this article with tears in your eyes, let this become your prayer:

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have wanted for so long. You know how many times I have cried. You know the jealousy I have tried to hide and the disappointment I have struggled to confess. Forgive me where my longing has become an idol. Heal what bitterness has damaged. Teach me to rejoice with others without despising my own life. Help me trust Your wisdom without pretending that waiting is painless. Give me grace to obey You whether my circumstances change or not. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Let my deepest hope rest not in what I may receive, but in You, my Savior and Lord. Amen.”
And when the old ache returns tomorrow, as it sometimes does, remember this:
The prayer you are still waiting to see answered is not the measure of how deeply Christ has loved you. Look to the cross.
